questions.q: A loan advertises "9.9% APR representative". What does that guarantee you?
options: Nothing for certain: at least 51% of accepted applicants get 9.9% or less, others may be offered more
9.9% is the highest rate anyone pays
questions.why: Representative APR must be offered to at least 51% of people accepted. Up to 49% can get a higher rate.

questions.q: A card charges about {m} interest a month. You owe {b}. Roughly how much interest is added this month?
questions.why: {m} of {b} = {answer}. Leave it unpaid and next month you pay interest on that too.

questions.q: Paying only the minimum on a credit card is a cheap way to spread the cost.
questions.why: Most of each minimum payment is interest, so £1,500 at 30% APR on minimums takes over 23 years and about £3,080 in interest.

questions.q: How do you use a credit card without paying any interest on purchases?
options: Pay the full balance every month
questions.why: Clear the full statement balance each month (a direct debit makes this automatic). Cash withdrawals cost fees and interest from day one.

questions.q: Put these ways of borrowing £500 for a year in order, cheapest first (typical 2026 rates).
items: Credit card cleared in full each month
questions.why: Cleared cards cost nothing; personal loans are cheaper than overdrafts; payday loans are the dearest even with the FCA cap.

questions.q: Which is the best way to start building a credit record at 18?
options: Register to vote and use a small credit card, paid in full by direct debit
Apply for several cards in one week to see which accepts
Avoid all credit, phone contracts included
Pay interest on a card to show you can
questions.why: Being on the electoral roll and paying on time builds your file. Many applications leave hard searches; paying interest proves nothing extra.

questions.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Your record of borrowing and repaying
A full credit check that other lenders can see
An eligibility check that lenders can't see
The yearly cost of borrowing, including fees
questions.why: Use soft-search eligibility checkers before applying; each full application leaves a hard search.

questions.q: You stay {d} into an arranged overdraft for a whole year at 40% EAR. Roughly how much interest do you pay?
questions.why: 40% of {d} = {answer} over a year. Overdrafts are for short gaps, not long-term borrowing.

questions.q: Buy now, pay later plans can't affect your credit file because they're interest-free.
questions.why: BNPL is credit. Missed payments can bring fees and show on your credit file, and lenders working through shops have followed FCA rules since 15 July 2026.

questions.q: Explain why paying only the minimum on a credit card takes so long to clear the debt.

ideas.label: Most of each payment goes on interest, so the balance hardly falls
The minimum is tiny (about 1%) and shrinks as the balance shrinks, so it drags on for years

questions.model: Most of each minimum payment just covers that month's interest, and only about 1% of the balance is actually paid off. The minimum also shrinks as the balance shrinks, so the debt lasts for years and the interest can add up to more than you borrowed.
questions.why: Interest eats the payment; only a sliver reduces the debt.

tests.answer: Most of the payment goes on interest, so only a tiny bit comes off the balance and it takes years.
Because the minimum is only a small amount.

questions.q: You have £2,000 in savings earning 4.5% and £1,500 on a card charging 30% APR. Explain why paying off most of the card usually makes sense.

ideas.label: The card costs far more in interest than the savings earn
Keep a small emergency buffer so a surprise doesn't add new debt

questions.model: The card charges about 30% while the savings earn about 4.5%, so every pound moved from savings to the card saves far more than it earned. Keep a small emergency buffer, though, so a surprise doesn't go straight back on the card.
questions.why: Clearing 30% debt is like a 30% risk-free return.

tests.answer: The card charges 30% which is far more than the 4.5% savings earn, but keep a small emergency buffer.
Because the card interest is much more than the savings interest.
